source_text: Τὰ μὲν γὰρ πόρρωθεν ἀφεστῶτα μικρότερά πως ὁρῶμεν, οἷς δ' ἂν μᾶλλον ἐγγίσωμεν, μᾶλλον αὐτῶν τὸ μέγεθος ἐξευρίσκομεν. Τῷ δὲ ἡλίῳ οὐδείς ἐστιν ἐγγυτέρω καὶ οὐδεὶς πορρωτέρω, ἀλλὰ ἀπ' ἴσου τοῦ διαστήματος τοῖς κατὰ πᾶν μέρος τῆς γῆς κατῳκισμένοις προσβάλλει. Σημεῖον δὲ, ὅτι καὶ Ἰνδοὶ καὶ Βρεττανοὶ τὸν ἴσον βλέπουσιν. Οὔτε γὰρ τοῖς τὴν ἑῴαν οἰκοῦσι καταδυόμενος τοῦ μεγέθους ὑφίησιν, οὔτε τοῖς πρὸς δυσμαῖς κατῳκισμένοις ἀνατέλλων ἐλάττων φαίνεται· οὔτε μὴν ἐν τῷ μεσουρανήματι γινόμενος, τῆς ἐφ' ἑκάτερα ὄψεως παραλλάττει. Μὴ ἐξαπατάτω σε τὸ φαινόμενον· μηδ' ὅτι πηχυαῖος τοῖς ὁρῶσι δοκεῖ, τοσοῦτον αὐτὸν εἶναι λογίσῃ. Συναιρεῖσθαι γὰρ πέφυκεν ἐν τοῖς μεγίστοις διαστήμασι τὰ μεγέθη τῶν ὁρωμένων, τῆς ὁρατικῆς δυνάμεως οὐκ ἐξικνουμένης τὸν μεταξὺ τόπον διαπερᾶν, ἀλλ' οἱονεὶ ἐνδαπανωμένης τῷ μέσῳ, καὶ κατ' ὀλίγον αὐτῆς μέρος προσβαλλούσης τοῖς ὁρατοῖς. Μικρὰ οὖν ἡ ὄψις ἡμῶν γινομένη, μικρὰ ἐποίησε νομίζεσθαι τὰ ὁρώμενα, τὸ οἰκεῖον πάθος τοῖς ὁρατοῖς ἐπιφέρουσα. Ὥστε ψεύδεται ἡ ὄψις, ἄπιστον τὸ κριτήριον. Ὑπομνήσθητι δὲ τῶν οἰκείων παθῶν, καὶ παρὰ σεαυτοῦ ἕξεις τῶν λεγομένων τὴν πίστιν. Εἴ ποτε ἀπὸ ἀκρωρείας μεγάλης πεδίον εἶδες πολύ τε καὶ ὕπτιον, ἡλίκα μέν σοι τῶν βοῶν κατεφάνη τὰ ζεύγη; πηλίκοι δὲ οἱ ἀροτῆρες αὐτοί; Εἰ μὴ μυρμήκων τινά σοι παρέσχον φαντασίαν; Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἀπὸ σκοπιᾶς ἐπὶ μέγα πέλαγος τετραμμένης τῇ θαλάσσῃ τὰς ὄψεις ἐπέβαλες, ἡλίκαι μέν σοι ἔδοξαν εἶναι τῶν νήσων αἱ μέγισται; πηλίκη δέ σοι κατεφάνη μία τῶν μυριοφόρων ὁλκάδων λευκοῖς ἱστίοις ὑπὲρ κυανῆς κομιζομένη θαλάσσης; Εἰ μὴ πάσης περιστερᾶς μικροτέραν σοι παρέσχετο τὴν φαντασίαν; Διότι, καθάπερ ἔφην, ἐνδαπανηθεῖσα τῷ ἀέρι ἡ ὄψις, ἐξίτηλος γινομένη, πρὸς τὴν ἀκριβῆ κατάληψιν τῶν ὁρωμένων οὐκ ἐξαρκεῖ. Ἤδη δέ που καὶ τῶν ὀρῶν τὰ μέγιστα βαθείαις φάραγξιν ἐκτετμημένα, περιφερῆ καὶ λεῖα ἡ ὄψις εἶναί φησι, ταῖς ἐξοχαῖς προσβάλλουσα μόναις, ταῖς δὲ μεταξὺ κοιλότησιν ἐμβῆναι δι' ἀτονίαν μὴ δυναμένη. Οὕτως οὐδὲ τὰ σχήματα τῶν σωμάτων ὁποῖά ἐστι διασώζει, ἀλλὰ περιφερεῖς οἴεται εἶναι τοὺς τετραγώνους τῶν πύργων. Ὥστε πανταχόθεν δῆλον, ὅτι ἐν ταῖς μεγίσταις ἀποστάσεσιν οὐκ ἔναρθρον ἀλλὰ συγκεχυμένην τῶν σωμάτων λαμβάνει τὴν εἰκασίαν. Μέγας οὖν ὁ φωστὴρ, κατὰ τὴν τῆς Γραφῆς μαρτυρίαν, καὶ ἀπειροπλασίων τοῦ φαινομένου. 6.10 Κἀκεῖνο δέ σοι ἐναργὲς ἔστω τοῦ μεγέθους σημεῖον. Ἀπείρων ὄντων τῷ πλήθει τῶν κατ' οὐρανὸν ἀστέρων, τὸ παρ' αὐτῶν συνερανιζόμενον φῶς οὐκ ἐξαρκεῖ τῆς νυκτὸς τὴν κατήφειαν διαλῦσαι. Μόνος δὲ οὗτος ὑπερφανεὶς τοῦ ὁρίζοντος, μᾶλλον δὲ ἔτι καὶ προσδοκώμενος, πρὶν καὶ ὑπερσχεῖν ὅλως τῆς γῆς, ἠφάνισε μὲν τὸ σκότος, ὑπερηύγασε δὲ τοὺς ἀστέρας, καὶ πεπηγότα τέως καὶ συμπεπιλημένον τὸν περὶ γῆν ἀέρα κατέτηξε καὶ διέχεεν. Ὅθεν καὶ ἄνεμοι ἑωθινοὶ καὶ δρόσοι ἐν αἰθρίᾳ τὴν γῆν περιρρέουσι. Τοσαύτην δὲ οὖσαν τὴν γῆν πῶς ἂν ἠδυνήθη ἐν μιᾷ καιροῦ ῥοπῇ τὴν πᾶσαν καταφωτίζειν, εἰ μὴ ἀπὸ μεγάλου τοῦ κύκλου τὴν αὐγὴν ἐπηφίει; Ἐνταῦθά μοι τὴν σοφίαν τοῦ τεχνίτου κατάμαθε, πῶς τῷ διαστήματι τούτῳ σύμμετρον ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ τὴν θερμότητα.
thought_title: The sun's apparent size and true greatness
orientation: Basil is explaining why the sun's apparent smallness to human eyes does not disprove its true vastness, arguing from the limits of sight over great distances.
pass_a_gloss: For things standing far off we see somehow smaller, but to whatever things we draw nearer, the more we discover their size. But for the sun no one is nearer and no one farther off, but from an equal distance it strikes those settled in every part of the earth. And a sign is that both Indians and Britons see it equal. For neither when setting does it diminish its size for those dwelling in the east, nor when rising does it appear smaller to those settled toward the west; nor indeed when it comes to be in mid-heaven does it alter from the appearance on either side. Let not the appearance deceive you; and do not reckon it to be so great because it seems a cubit to those seeing it. For the sizes of things seen are naturally contracted in the greatest distances, since the visual power does not suffice to pass through the space between, but is as it were used up in the middle, and with a small part of itself strikes the visible things. So our sight becoming small made the things seen be thought small, bringing its own condition to bear upon the visible things. So the sight lies, the criterion is untrustworthy. And remember your own experiences, and from yourself you will have proof of the things said. If ever from a great mountain peak you saw a plain both broad and flat, how large did the teams of oxen appear to you? And how big the plowmen themselves? Did they not present to you some appearance of ants? And if also from a lookout turned toward a great sea you cast your eyes upon the sea, how large did the greatest of the islands seem to you to be? And how big did one of the ten-thousand-burden cargo ships appear to you, carried with white sails over the dark-blue sea? Did it not present to you an appearance smaller than every dove? Because, just as I said, the sight being used up in the air, becoming faint, does not suffice for the exact apprehension of the things seen. And already somewhere also the greatest of mountains cut through with deep ravines, the sight says them to be rounded and smooth, striking only the projections, and not being able through weakness to enter into the hollows between. Thus it does not even preserve the shapes of bodies as they are, but thinks the square towers to be round. So from every side it is clear that in the greatest distances it receives not a distinct but a confused impression of bodies. Great therefore is the light, according to the testimony of the Scripture, and infinitely greater than what appears. 6.10 And let this also be a clear sign to you of its size. Though the stars in heaven are infinite in number, the light gathered together from them does not suffice to dissolve the gloom of the night. But this one alone appearing above the horizon, or rather even while still expected, before it has risen wholly above the earth, made the darkness vanish, outshone the stars, and melted and dispersed the air around the earth that was until then frozen and packed together. From which also morning winds and dews in clear weather flow around the earth. And the earth being so great, how could it have been able to illuminate it all in one moment of time, if it did not cast its ray from a great circle? Here learn the wisdom of the craftsman, how he gave it heat commensurate with this distance.

choices.why: The source uses the specific measurement 'cubit' for the sun's apparent size; keeping it preserves the concrete image Basil invokes.
Basil's metaphor is that visual power is consumed or spent in the intervening space; 'used up' conveys the exhaustion of the faculty.
The compound literally means 'carrying ten thousand burdens,' indicating a very large merchant vessel; the literal rendering preserves the hyperbolic scale.
The perfect participle from συμπιλέω means compressed or packed tight; 'packed together' captures the dense, congealed state of the air before the sun disperses it.
The compound means 'infinitely many times more'; 'infinitely greater' conveys the rhetorical force of the sun's true size exceeding all appearance.

pass_b_english: For things that stand far off we see as somehow smaller, and the closer we draw to them, the more we discover their true size. But with the sun, no one is closer and no one farther away; it strikes those settled in every part of the earth from an equal distance. A proof of this is that both Indians and Britons see it the same. For it does not diminish in size as it sets for those who live in the east, nor does it appear smaller as it rises for those settled toward the west; and when it is at mid-heaven, it does not differ from the view on either side. Do not let the appearance deceive you, and do not reckon that because it seems a cubit long to those who see it, it is actually that size. For the sizes of visible things naturally contract at great distances, since the power of sight cannot cross the intervening space, but is, as it were, used up in the middle, and only a small part of it reaches the visible objects. So our sight becomes small, and it makes the things seen be thought small, imposing its own condition on what is visible. Therefore sight lies, and its judgment is untrustworthy. But recall your own experiences, and you will have from yourself the proof of what I am saying. If you have ever seen from a high mountain peak a plain that is broad and level, how large did the teams of oxen appear to you? How big were the plowmen themselves? Did they not give you the impression of ants? And if from a lookout turned toward the open sea you cast your eyes upon the water, how large did the greatest of the islands seem to you? How big did one of the ten-thousand-burden cargo ships appear, carried over the dark blue sea with white sails? Did it not present an impression smaller than any dove? Because, as I said, sight is used up in the air, becomes faint, and is not sufficient for an accurate grasp of what is seen. And indeed, the greatest mountains, cut through with deep ravines, sight declares to be round and smooth, because it reaches only the projections and through weakness cannot enter the hollows between. So it does not even preserve the shapes of bodies as they are, but thinks square towers are round. Thus it is clear from every side that at the greatest distances sight receives not a distinct but a confused impression of bodies. Great, then, is the light, according to the testimony of Scripture, and infinitely greater than what appears.

And let this also be a clear sign to you of its size. Though the stars in heaven are countless in number, the light gathered from them is not enough to dissolve the gloom of night. But this one alone, appearing above the horizon—or rather, even while still expected, before it has fully risen over the earth—makes the darkness vanish, outshines the stars, and melts and disperses the air around the earth that had been fixed and packed together. From this come the morning winds and the dews that flow over the earth in clear weather. And how could it illuminate the whole earth, vast as it is, in a single moment of time, unless it cast its radiance from a great circle? Here learn the wisdom of the craftsman: how he gave it heat proportionate to this distance.

last_rejected.why: κυανῆς means dark/black, not blue; ancient Greek κύανος is black/dark, misleads on color perception
last_rejected.fix: the dark sea or the black sea
last_rejected.ruling: κυανῆς can mean dark blue; 'dark blue sea' is within normal range, not a misleading error.

last_rejected.why: ἠφάνισε is stronger than vanish; it means destroyed/obliterated, emphasizing total elimination
last_rejected.fix: destroyed the darkness or obliterated the darkness
last_rejected.ruling: ἠφάνισε includes 'vanish/destroy'; rendering 'makes vanish' is within normal range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.why: Missing 'κατήφειαν' (dejection/gloom as emotional quality); 'gloom' alone loses the personification of night as mournful
last_rejected.fix: the gloom and dejection of night
last_rejected.ruling: κατήφειαν means gloom/darkness here; 'gloom of night' captures it adequately in context.
